title.en: Ramayana — Sundara Kanda (Wikipedia Simplified Story — English, Full Text)

lessons.title: Lesson 01 — Hanuman's Leap Across the Ocean
lessons.content:
Hanuman increased his body to the size of a mountain and ascended Mount Mahendra, ready to leap across the ocean. He bowed to the Sun, Indra, Brahma, and all living beings. Tightening his calves and clenching his fists, he leaped in one powerful surge. The mountain split due to the force of his take-off. Like a cloud in the sky, or a released arrow of Rama, Hanuman swiftly moved towards Lanka.

Desiring to assist Rama's mission, the mountain Mainaka, who was on the path, requested him to rest upon its peak. Hanuman politely declined the hospitality and proceeded. Surasa, the mother of the Nagas, wanting to test Hanuman, blocked his way by opening her mouth like a cave of death. Hanuman cleverly entered her mouth, immediately came out again, received her blessings, and continued on his way. A female rakshasa named Simhika, who could catch shadows, began pulling Hanuman by his shadow. Hanuman darted into her stomach with the speed of an arrow, tore her belly open, and landed on the Trikuta mountain peak in Lanka like an unimpeded arrow of Rama.

lessons.title: Lesson 02 — Entry into the City of Lanka
lessons.content: Hanuman was astonished by the splendor, beauty, and secure system of the city of Lanka as he observed it from a distance. After nightfall, he assumed a small form and attempted to enter the city. Lankini, the presiding deity of the city of Lanka, obstructed him at the entrance. Hanuman struck her. Lankini realized that he was a divine-born being and that, as Brahma had foretold, misfortune was about to befall Lanka. Instead of passing through the gate, Hanuman leaped over the rampart, placing his left foot first, and entered Lanka, the magnificent creation of Maya, and began searching for Sita. At that time, the moon rose, making the city of Lanka even more beautiful.

lessons.title: Lesson 03 — Search for Sita in the Inner Palace
lessons.content:
Assuming a small form, Hanuman searched for Sita everywhere: in Ravana's palace, in the drinking hall, and in the Pushpaka Vimana. During the night, the women in Ravana's palace were indulging in pleasures and were asleep in strange and varied postures. Disturbed by these sights, Hanuman reassured himself that since he was pursuing Rama's mission without succumbing to any vices and was engaged in the search for Sita, no fault would attach to him, nor would his vow of celibacy be broken. He was amazed by the beauty of the Pushpaka Vimana and the wealth of Ravana. He mistook Mandodari among the sleeping women for Sita. He soon corrected his mistake and continued his search. He grieved when he couldn't find any trace of Sita. He didn't know what to do. He didn't want to return empty-handed and disappoint everyone. He worried that Sugriva, Rama, Lakshmana, and many others would be distraught if his mission failed. He even contemplated suicide. He resolved not to return without finding Sita. At that moment, the Ashoka Vana (Ashoka Grove) came into view.

He prayed: "Namo'stu Ramaya Salakshmanaya, Devyai cha Tasyai Janakatmajayi, Namo'stu Rudrendra Yamanilebhyo, Namo'stu Chandrarka Marudganebhyah" (Salutations to Rama and Lakshmana, and to the Goddess, the daughter of Janaka. Salutations to Rudra, Indra, Yama, and Vayu. Salutations to the Moon, Sun, and Marut Ganas). He requested the gods and great sages to grant him success in his mission. He prayed to Brahma, Agni, Vayu Deva, Indra, Varuna, Surya, Chandra, the Ashwini Devas, the Maruts, Shiva, all beings, and Sri Maha Vishnu to grant him success and entered the Ashoka Vana in search of Sita.

lessons.title: Lesson 04 — Sighting Sita in Ashoka Vana
lessons.content:
The Ashoka Vana was uncommonly beautiful. It contained lovely trees, flowers, strangely constructed artificial mountains, and streams of water. It had jewel-studded lakes and magnificent Chaitya-Prasadas (temple-like mansions). Hanuman climbed an exceptionally beautiful Shinsupa tree within the Vana and began to observe the surroundings.

There, beneath the Shinsupa tree, he saw a woman tormented by female rakshasas, emaciated and fearful like a deer surrounded by lions. She was clad in a single garment, resembling a flame covered in smoke, or reputation ruined by false accusations, or the moon veiled by clouds. Based on the ornaments she wore, her demeanor, and her current state, Hanuman confirmed that she was Sita. Reflecting on her pitiful condition and the sorrow of Rama and Lakshmana, he grieved, concluding that time is a formidable and insurmountable force for anyone.

lessons.title: Lesson 05 — Trijata's Dream
lessons.content:
Ravana, driven by lust, arrived and threatened Sita, ordering her to yield to him. Sita placed a blade of grass between them and condemned Ravana's unrighteousness and cowardice. She warned him that this vile intention was upon him because his end was near. She firmly told Ravana that Lanka would surely be reduced to ashes by the fire of Sri Rama's arrows. Ravana set a deadline of one month and departed. The female rakshasas began trying to persuade Sita to agree, either through kind words or threats. They threatened to eat her if she did not submit to Ravana. Sita, overwhelmed by fear and having lost all hope, resolved to take her own life.

Among them, a kind-hearted rakshasa woman named Trijata rebuked the other female rakshasas, warning them that harming a virtuous woman like Sita would bring ruin to the rakshasa race. She recounted a dream she had:

"Rama and Lakshmana came to Lanka in a white palanquin pulled by a thousand swans with elephant tusks. Sita was seated on the peak of a white mountain. She touched the Sun and the Moon. Sita was seated on Rama's lap, riding a white elephant with four tusks. The divine elephant carrying Sita, Rama, and Lakshmana stood in the sky above Lanka. Rama appeared in Lanka, dressed in white, with Sita and Lakshmana, in a chariot pulled by eight bulls. Afterwards, they all boarded the Pushpaka Vimana and flew northwards.

"Ravana, wearing red clothes, smeared with oil, and intoxicated, fell from the Pushpaka Vimana. He was in a chariot pulled by donkeys. A black-clad woman tied a rope around his neck and dragged him southwards. He fell into a foul-smelling cesspit. Ravana rode a pig, Kumbhakarna rode a large camel, and Indrajit rode a crocodile, all going south. Vibhishana, however, was in the sky with a white umbrella, divine ornaments, riding a white elephant, and accompanied by his ministers. The city of Lanka was destroyed and fell into the ocean. All the female rakshasas were drinking oil and leaping wildly around Lanka like mad women."

After narrating this, Trijata advised the other female rakshasas to beg Sita Devi to protect them from danger. The rakshasa women were terrified upon hearing the dreadful dream. Auspicious omens began to appear for Sita, who had been ready to commit suicide.

lessons.title: Lesson 06 — Description of Sri Rama
lessons.content:
Observing all this from the tree, Hanuman surmised that any further delay might cause Sita to take her life. However, he worried that if he appeared suddenly, she might panic and cry out, which would ruin the mission. From the tree, he slowly began to narrate the story of Rama, the son of Dasaratha. In the course of the story, he revealed that he was one of the messengers sent by Rama to search for Sita and that he had reached Lanka and was currently watching her from the tree. Sita was somewhat delighted by the sound of the Rama-katha. But she was confused, thinking she might be dreaming. She lifted her head and was alarmed to see the Vanara, who shone like a streak of lightning or an Ashoka flower. She bowed to Brahma, Mahendra, Brihaspati, and Agni, praying that what she had heard might be true. Hanuman slowly climbed down the tree and wished her well. He explained his background and Rama's sorrow to Sita. Praising Sri Rama's valor and noble qualities, he spoke comforting words, assuring her that she would soon be liberated. Sita wept, inquired about the well-being of everyone, and then asked him to describe Rama.

Hanuman, with devotion, described the incomparably handsome Rama and his brother Lakshmana. "Rama has long arms reaching his knees (Ajanubahu). His eyes are like lotus petals (Kamala Patraksha). He is endowed with beauty and compassion, possesses auspicious marks, is full of brilliance (Tejomurti), a protector of Dharma, proficient in all knowledge, and follows the ways of the world (Lokamaryadalu). He has well-proportioned limbs. He has long arms, a conch-like neck, and joints covered with muscles. He has three firm places, three long limbs, three equal limbs, and three reddish limbs. He possesses fourteen symmetrical limbs. He has four kinds of gait. He is the best, a hero, and dark-complexioned. His brother Lakshmana possesses the same auspicious characteristics, but has a reddish complexion. Such Rama and Lakshmana are grieving for you. They have befriended Sugriva and dispatched Vanaras in all directions to search for you. O Sita Devi! Sri Rama will soon take you from this place," Hanuman told her.

Upon hearing about Sri Rama, Sita was comforted. Hanuman then presented her with Rama's signet ring (Anguliyakam) as an identifier. He conveyed the words spoken by Rama. He wished her well. He requested to take her with him if she wished. Sita was pleased with Hanuman's words and praised his valor. However, she said that Sri Rama himself should come, defeat Ravana, and take her back. She stated that Rama's valor was unmatched in the three worlds. She asked Hanuman to convey her regards to Rama, Lakshmana, Sugriva, and the bear and monkey warriors, according to Dharma. Sita gave Hanuman some identifiers, narrating the story of Kakasura. She blessed Hanuman and gave him her head-jewel (Chudamani) as a token. She said she would not live if Rama did not rescue her within one month. She expressed doubt about how others (except Hanuman, Vayu Deva, and Garuda) could cross the great ocean.

In response, Hanuman convinced her that there were many great heroes among the Vanaras who were superior to him, and he, being an ordinary one, was sent first for the messenger's task (not for war). He assured her that the mighty Rama and Lakshmana, accompanied by the armies of the Vanaras and bears, would soon arrive in Lanka, destroy it like the Sun and Moon or Agni and Vayu, and eliminate Ravana. Sita Devi blessed Hanuman.

lessons.title: Lesson 07 — Punishing the Rakshasas
lessons.content:
Contented by the sight of Sita, Hanuman resolved to speak with Ravana and inspect Lanka as part of the mission. This would allow him to warn Ravana and learn about Lanka's defense system. Moreover, he could inflict as much damage as possible on Lanka in the process. With this resolve, Hanuman immediately assumed a fierce form, destroyed the Vana and the thousands of rakshasas who opposed him, and sat atop the Makara Torana (arched gateway).

Ravana sent eighty thousand soldiers to capture the Vanara. Hanuman shouted the victory cry: "Jayatyatibalo Ramo, Lakshmanascha Mahabalah, Raja Jayati Sugrivo, Raghavenaabhipaalitah, Dasoham Kosalendrasya, Ramasyaaklishta Karmanah, Hanuman Shatru Sainyanam Nihanta Marutatmajah" (Victory to the extremely mighty Sri Rama. Victory to the very valorous Lakshmana. Victory to Sugriva, the King of Kishkindha, who is protected by Raghava. I am the servant of the King of Kosala, Rama, whose actions are unblemished. I am Hanuman, the son of Vayu, the destroyer of enemy armies). He continued, "Even a thousand Ravanas cannot withstand me in battle. I will destroy all the rakshasas and the city of Lanka with thousands of stones and trees. I will complete my task, bow to Mother Sita, and leave. Let the rakshasas watch helplessly." Roaring thus, Hanuman beat all the rakshasas with the iron bar that fastened the main gate. He increased his body to the size of a mountain, knocked down the Chaitya Prasada, and used a large pillar from the Prasada as a mace (Parigha) to strike down everyone.

Then, Ravana sent Jambumali, the very powerful son of Prahasta. Jambumali's body was crushed by the mace in Hanuman's hand. Following him, seven sons of ministers, skilled in the art of war and blazing like fire, attacked Hanuman with a large army. Hanuman roared fearfully and killed some with his palms, some with his fists, and others with his sharp claws, scattering the enemies' blood and flesh across the battlefield. After that, great army commanders like Virupaksha, Yupaksha, Durdhara, Praghassa, and Bhaskarna attacked Hanuman, who was seated at the entrance of the Vana, with their forces. They were all killed by Hanuman. The battlefield was filled with the corpses of rakshasas and their vehicles, as well as weapon and chariot fragments.

Next, the mighty and powerful Akshakumara, who was blessed with boons and owned a great chariot, approached Hanuman with all his forces. The battle between them astonished the gods and anti-gods (Suras and Asuras). Akshakumara's arrows, like a downpour, greatly wounded Hanuman. Hanuman was impressed by his valor. He hesitated to kill such a valiant and brilliant warrior. But knowing that if he neglected him, he would face defeat, Hanuman went into a frenzy. Leaping into the sky and moving with the speed of wind, he clapped his hands and killed Akshakumara's horses. Then, like Garuda seizing a great serpent, he firmly grasped Akshakumara by the legs, swung him around, and dashed him to the ground. Akshakumara's body was completely pulverized.

Learning of this, Ravana was agitated. Giving him many instructions, he sent Indrajit to battle. Indrajit was blessed with a boon from Brahma, a warrior whose valor even Indra and others could not restrain, and an expert in mantra and tantra warfare. He bowed to his father, filled with the excitement of battle, and rode alone on a divine chariot towards Hanuman without an army. The battle between them, fought in strange and varied ways, caused panic among all celestial beings. Both realized that conquering the other was impossible. Concluding that there was no other way, and resolving to at least bind the Vanara, Indrajit launched the Brahmastra. It bound Hanuman. According to the boon granted to Hanuman by Brahma, the arrow did not harm him and was dispelled the next moment. Yet, as a mark of respect for Lord Brahma, Hanuman pretended to be bound by the Astra. He wished to converse with Ravana in this manner. The rakshasa forces bound and tormented Hanuman and led him to Ravana's court.

lessons.title: Lesson 08 — Conversation with Ravana
lessons.content:
Pretending to be subdued by the Brahmastra, Hanuman entered Ravana's court and saw Ravana. Ravanasura's court was splendidly adorned with jewels. Ravana's crown, ornaments, clothes, and anointing substances were magnificent. Ravana, a great splendor and hero, shone with his ten heads, like the Mandara mountain with its peaks inhabited by many cruel beasts. He was seated on a high, jewel-studded throne. Surrounded by four ministers skilled in diplomacy, he resembled a mountain of kohl. Then Hanuman thought: 'Alas! This Ravana's form is wonderful. His courage is unparalleled. His strength is praiseworthy. His radiance is unmatched. Truly, this king of the rakshasas is adorned with all auspicious marks. If he had not embarked on this unrighteous path, he would have been the ruler of even the realm of the Suras. All worlds fear him. If he were angry, he is capable of submerging the entire universe in the ocean and creating a deluge!'

Ravana ordered his ministers to find out who Hanuman was, why he had come, and who had sent him. Hanuman spoke to Ravana thus: 'O King! I am the minister of Sugriva and the messenger of Rama. I am a Vanara named Hanuman. Sugriva, in a gesture of friendship, asked me to inquire about your well-being. You have made a grave mistake by bringing Rama's wife, Sita. Because of this, all the merit you have accumulated will become fruitless. Rama himself killed Vali. Neither you nor anyone else can withstand the force of Rama's arrows. This evil deed has brought disaster upon you and Lanka. Rama is a man. You are a rakshasa. I am a Vanara, and I have no partiality. Therefore, listen to my words, return Sita, and seek refuge with Rama. No one in the three worlds can protect one who has incurred Rama's wrath,' he advised.

Ravana became angry and ordered the Vanara to be killed. At that moment, Vibhishana intervened, saying: 'It is not the duty of a king to kill a messenger (Rajadharma). Moreover, if he does not return, you will lose the opportunity to fight and defeat your enemies. Therefore, he suggested punishing him and then releasing him. Calmed slightly by those words, Ravana commanded that the Vanara's tail be set on fire and that he be paraded throughout the city.

lessons.title: Lesson 09 — The Burning of Lanka
lessons.content:
Ravana, enraged, ordered Hanuman's tail to be set on fire. The rakshasa servants wrapped old cloths around Hanuman's tail and set it ablaze. They began parading him throughout the city. Taking this opportunity, Hanuman thoroughly inspected the city of Lanka. Hearing the news, Sita Devi prayed to the God of Fire (Agni Deva) to be cool towards Hanuman. Realizing that the absence of pain despite his tail burning was due to Sita's glory and the kindness of Agni, who was the friend of his father Vayu Deva, Hanuman resolved to offer Lanka as an oblation to that fire. He broke his bonds and beat the crowd of rakshasas with a Parigha (iron mace). Leaping high, he blazed forth like the rising Sun. Starting with Prahasta's house, he set fire to the magnificent buildings in Lanka. He burned down the buildings in Lanka, sparing only Vibhishana's house.

Suddenly, Hanuman remembered Sita's situation and was struck with dismay. He was overwhelmed by the thought that his rashness might have caused Sita to be consumed by the fire along with Lanka. He wept for the harm his impulsiveness had caused to his race and his mission and was ready to take his own life. However, he was relieved to learn that Sita was safe. He visited Sita one more time, spoke words of comfort to her, and promised that Rama would soon arrive with the entire Vanara army. He bowed to her and set out towards the north. 

Thus, Hanuman, as Rama's messenger, crossed the ocean, found Sita, killed the rakshasas, terrified Lanka, crushed Ravana's arrogance, brought solace to Sita, and ascended Mount Arishta for his return journey.

lessons.title: Lesson 10 — The Return Leap
lessons.content:
With the stamping of Hanuman's feet, Mount Arishta sank into the ground. Hanuman effortlessly crossed the sky like a great ship traversing the ocean. On the way, he respectfully touched Mainaka mountain, and as he neared the northern shore of the ocean, he roared loudly. Hearing that shout, Jambavan and others realized it was Hanuman's proclamation of victory and began leaping with joy. Like a cloud, Hanuman descended upon Mount Mahendra and bowed to the elders like Jambavan, his teachers, and the young prince Angada. "I have found Mother Sita; she is held captive by rakshasas, is emaciated, and is waiting for Rama," Hanuman announced. The word "found" filled all the Vanaras with extreme joy. They embraced him and danced with happiness. Hanuman then elaborated to his group on all the details of his visit to the city of Lanka.

Angada suggested that they should all go, destroy Lanka, defeat Ravana, bring Sita, and hand her over to Rama. But Jambavan restrained him, saying that the correct course of action was first to report the news to Rama and Sugriva. All of them eagerly set out for Kishkindha.

lessons.title: Lesson 11 — Madhuvana
lessons.content:
The Vanaras, led by Angada, were full of enthusiasm because the trace of Sita was found, and they headed towards Kishkindha surrounding Hanuman. On the way, they reached the beautiful Madhuvana (Honey Grove). It belonged to Sugriva and was protected by the aged Vanara hero Dadhikukha. With Angada's permission, all the Vanaras began to pick and eat the fruits, drink the honey, leap around, and madly destroy the Vana in their intoxication. They severely beat Dadhikukha when he tried to stop them. Dadhikukha, helpless, flew quickly to Sugriva with his fellow forest guards and complained about the outrage.

Sugriva surmised that his servants, the Vanaras, would not dare to do such a thing unless the mission to find Sita had been successful. Sugriva told Rama and Lakshmana that Dadhikukha was implicitly signaling the success of the Sita search mission under the pretext of the Vana's destruction, and that there was an opportunity to hear good news. He congratulated Dadhikukha for bringing the good news. Dadhikukha returned to Madhuvana, spoke kindly to Angada and others, and asked them to quickly go to Sugriva. Angada, Hanuman, and the rest of the group flew swiftly into the sky like a tempest towards Sugriva.

lessons.title: Lesson 12 — Informing Rama of Sita's Whereabouts
lessons.content:
Angada, Hanuman, and other prominent Vanaras landed with great enthusiasm on Prasravana Hill, where Sugriva, Rama, and Lakshmana were. As soon as Hanuman said, "Drishta Devi" (I have seen the Goddess), Rama and Lakshmana were filled with immense joy. Lakshmana, who had faith in Hanuman's achievement, looked affectionately at Sugriva. Encouraged by the other Vanaras, Hanuman turned towards the south, bowed to Mother Sita, presented the Chudamani (head-jewel) she had given him to Rama, and narrated the entire account of his leap across the ocean to Rama, Lakshmana, and Sugriva.

O Rama! Mother Sita has her hair in a single braid (Ekaveni), is miserable in the confinement of the rakshasa women, and constantly remembers only you. She inquired about the well-being of everyone. She is alive only in the hope that you will soon come, free her, and take her. She said she would not live if that did not happen within one month. Rama! I comforted her by telling her that she would soon see Rama, who has the valor of a lion, and Lakshmana, who holds the bow, at the gate of Lanka. I have returned after consoling her with auspicious words,' Hanuman reported to Sri Rama.

(From the first Sarga of Yuddha Kanda) - Hearing Hanuman's words, Sri Rama was pleased and spoke thus: "The great deeds performed by Hanuman are the most wonderful in the world. Unimaginable. Unachievable by others. There is no one equal to Hanuman in splendor and strength. A servant who not only accomplishes a difficult task for his master but also achieves other related tasks without harming the primary one is the best. Through the accomplishment of this task, Hanuman has saved the lives of all of us. I am unable to repay Hanuman for such a great service. I can only offer the happiness of a tight embrace. This is all I can give now, my everything," saying thus, Sri Rama, with a thrill in his body, clasped Hanuman, who had successfully completed the task entrusted to him and returned pure in spirit, to his heart.

(From the Adhyatma Ramayana: Those who worship the lotus feet of Sri Rama with Tulsi leaves and other offerings attain the supreme state unmatched by others. That very Sri Ramachandra, the embodiment of merit, blessed Hanuman and personally granted him the joy of his embrace. How can we fully praise the fortune of that Maruthi - Translation from Gita Press, Gorakhpur publication).
